title: How Tsunamis Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how tsunamis work: the word's etymology, wave anatomy (crest, trough, wave height, wave length, wave period), how wind-driven waves form versus tsunamis, how underwater earthquakes from plate tectonics and subduction generate tsunamis, tsunami speed in deep versus shallow water, drawback, harbor resonance and the wraparound effect, the 2004 Indian Ocean and 2011 Japan tsunamis, the Fukushima nuclear meltdown triggered by the tsunami, tsunami early warning systems, and effects on marine life. The episode also includes a Salt Lake City/Phoenix/Australia tour announcement, a brief off-topic banter segment, and a listener mail story about a strawberry farmer's family and a cremation box.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Tour announcement and opening banter
segments.summary: The hosts announce tour dates in Salt Lake City, Phoenix, Melbourne, Perth and Brisbane, then banter about the upcoming episode topic, a movie, and a Norm McDonald stand-up special.

segments.title: What a tsunami is and wave anatomy
segments.summary: The hosts define tsunami from the Japanese word meaning harbor and waves, note tsunamis can be as high as 100 feet and travel up to about 300 to 600 miles per hour, and describe wave anatomy: crest, trough, wave height, wave length and wave period.

segments.title: Wind-generated waves and undertow
segments.summary: The hosts discuss undertow briefly, then explain that everyday ocean waves are generated by wind transferring kinetic energy through water, with capillary waves forming first.

segments.title: Underwater earthquakes and plate tectonics
segments.summary: Tsunamis usually begin with underwater earthquakes. The hosts explain tectonic plates floating on the asthenosphere, plate boundaries, subduction at about 2.5 centimeters per year, and how an upward snap of a lighter plate sends energy through the water column, spreading outward like ripples from a pebble.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the discussion of tsunami speed.

segments.title: Tsunami speed, shoaling and the wave height near shore
segments.summary: Tsunamis move fastest in deep water and slow and grow taller near shore as the shelf shallows. Their waves extend down to the seafloor, and the approach to land can look like a very fast rising flood, sometimes with drawback where the trough arrives first.

segments.title: Harbor resonance, wraparound effect and sounds
segments.summary: The hosts describe harbor resonance as repeated oscillation that amplifies a tsunami in a harbor, and the wraparound effect in which a barrier island splits a tsunami wave and briefly amplifies it when the parts rejoin. They also mention the reported sound of a freight train or jet.

segments.title: 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and human stories
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the magnitude 9.1 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami, which killed about 230,000 people across eleven countries during the holiday season. They recount documentary filmmaker Dave Barnhart's follow-up work and the story of baby eighty one and the family that was denied aid after appearing on Good Morning America. They also mention the film The Impossible.

segments.title: 2011 Japan tsunami and Fukushima meltdown
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 2011 Japan tsunami, with a death toll around 20,000 and damage around 309 billion US dollars, the costliest natural disaster in history. They explain how the tsunami knocked out power at the Fukushima nuclear facility, cooling failed, and hydrogen explosions breached the reactor. They also discuss the reading list on the tsunami aftermath and a school that was swept away.

segments.title: Tsunami early warning and studying tsunamis
segments.summary: The hosts explain that tsunamis cannot be stopped, so early warning is key. Tide gauges, buoys, seismograph stations and eyewitness reports are used. Warnings are issued for underwater quakes of magnitude 7.5 or higher, and minutes of warning can help people reach higher ground.

segments.title: Tsunami effects on marine life
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how tsunamis damage the benthic ecosystem, coral reefs, seagrass beds and mangrove forests, and how they can carry invasive species across oceans. They admit they could not find what happens to whales hit by tsunamis and ask listeners.

segments.title: Tallest tsunami and Lituya Bay
segments.summary: The hosts note the tallest tsunami recorded, at Lituya Bay, Alaska, reaching about 1,720 feet, and point listeners to HowStuffWorks for more.

segments.title: Listener mail: strawberry farmer and the wooden box
segments.summary: A listener who runs a strawberry farm writes about her family's wooden box that was labeled as her grandfather after Hurricane Sandy damaged her grandmother's Long Island home. The hosts thank her and mention a Milwaukee show.
